title: Acute Respiratory Failure, ARDS & Mechanical Ventilation: Escalation, Lung Protection and Weaning
html:
Acute respiratory failure means the lungs cannot maintain adequate oxygenation, carbon-dioxide elimination, or both. It is a physiologic syndrome caused by another problem—not a final diagnosis. The RN recognizes failure before arrest, supports oxygenation and ventilation, treats reversible causes, prevents ventilator injury, and evaluates readiness to reduce support every day.

Learning goals

  • Differentiate hypoxemic, hypercapnic, and mixed respiratory failure.
  • Recognize fatigue and declining ventilation even when oxygen saturation appears acceptable.
  • Escalate oxygen, high-flow therapy, noninvasive support, and invasive ventilation safely.
  • Explain ARDS pathophysiology and lung-protective ventilation.
  • Respond systematically to high- and low-pressure ventilator alarms.
  • Prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia, delirium, immobility, and device injury.
  • Coordinate spontaneous awakening, breathing trials, and extubation readiness.

Respiratory failure is about gas exchange and work

Hypoxemic respiratory failure primarily reflects inadequate arterial oxygenation from V/Q mismatch, shunt, diffusion limitation, or low inspired oxygen. Pneumonia, pulmonary edema, ARDS, atelectasis, and pulmonary embolism are common mechanisms. Hypercapnic respiratory failure reflects inadequate alveolar ventilation and rising carbon dioxide, often from airflow obstruction, respiratory-muscle fatigue, central nervous system depression, neuromuscular weakness, chest-wall limitation, or excessive ventilatory demand. Mixed failure is common.

Pulse oximetry estimates oxygen saturation but does not measure ventilation or carbon dioxide. Supplemental oxygen can improve the displayed saturation while opioid toxicity, neuromuscular weakness, or fatigue continues to worsen. Interpret oxygenation with respiratory pattern and effort, level of consciousness, air movement, blood gases when indicated, and the clinical trajectory.

Recognize failure before apnea

Assess respiratory rate and pattern, speech, posture, accessory-muscle use, paradoxical movement, air entry, cough and secretions, oxygen device and flow, saturation trend, mental status, skin color, heart rate, blood pressure, and temperature. Review baseline disease, recent medications, aspiration, infection, trauma, procedures, and prior ventilatory support.

Escalate for severe or worsening hypoxemia, inability to speak, exhaustion, decreasing respiratory effort after intense distress, new agitation or somnolence, silent chest, weak cough, inability to protect the airway, hemodynamic instability, worsening acidosis, or rapidly rising carbon dioxide. A slowing rate in an exhausted client can be deterioration, not recovery.

Normal saturation does not prove adequate breathing
Ask two separate questions: Is oxygen entering the blood? Is the client moving enough air to eliminate carbon dioxide? Oxygenation and ventilation can fail independently.

Find and treat the reversible cause

Immediate causes may include mucus plugging, bronchospasm, pneumothorax, pulmonary edema, pneumonia, aspiration, sepsis, pulmonary embolism, opioid or sedative effect, upper-airway obstruction, equipment disconnection, or neuromuscular weakness. Stabilization and diagnosis proceed together. Position, open and support the airway, provide prescribed oxygen, monitor continuously when unstable, obtain ordered blood gases and imaging, and activate respiratory or critical-care expertise early.

Treatment is cause-specific: bronchodilation for bronchospasm, reversal and ventilation support for selected drug toxicity, diuresis or hemodynamic care for cardiogenic edema, antibiotics and source control for infection, pleural decompression for tension pneumothorax, and secretion removal for obstruction. Do not let a broad label such as “respiratory failure” replace causal reasoning.

Escalate oxygen according to response

Select an oxygen device that can reliably meet the prescribed target and inspiratory demand. Nasal cannula, simple or reservoir masks, air-entrainment devices, high-flow nasal oxygen, and positive-pressure support provide different flow, concentration, humidification, and pressure. Verify fit, source, flow, humidification when applicable, skin integrity, and actual client response.

High-flow nasal oxygen can deliver heated humidified high flow and may reduce work of breathing in selected hypoxemic clients. It does not protect an unprotected airway or guarantee adequate ventilation. Increasing support without improvement in effort, mentation, gas exchange, or hemodynamics should trigger timely escalation rather than prolonged delay before intubation.

Use noninvasive ventilation only when the client can participate safely

Continuous or bilevel positive airway pressure can improve oxygenation, recruit alveoli, and reduce work of breathing in selected clients, including many with cardiogenic pulmonary edema or acute hypercapnic COPD exacerbation. Success requires an appropriate diagnosis, a cooperative client, mask tolerance, manageable secretions, and close reassessment.

Noninvasive ventilation may be unsafe with respiratory arrest, inability to protect the airway, severe vomiting or aspiration risk, copious secretions, facial anatomy or injury that prevents a seal, profound agitation, or severe hemodynamic instability. Monitor mental status, respiratory effort, mask leak and pressure injury, gastric distention, synchrony, oxygenation, carbon dioxide and pH when indicated, and readiness for intubation. Failure must be recognized early.

ARDS is diffuse inflammatory lung injury

Acute respiratory distress syndrome develops after a known clinical insult such as pneumonia, sepsis, aspiration, trauma, pancreatitis, or transfusion-related injury. Inflammation damages the alveolar-capillary barrier, allowing protein-rich fluid into alveoli, reducing surfactant, causing atelectasis and stiff lungs, and producing severe V/Q mismatch and shunt.

Diagnosis integrates acute timing, bilateral imaging opacities, impaired oxygenation, and evidence that edema is not explained primarily by cardiac failure or fluid overload. Severity is commonly described using the PaO₂/FiO₂ relationship under specified respiratory support. ARDS is not diagnosed from a single chest image or low saturation alone.

Lung-protective ventilation limits additional injury

Mechanical ventilation supports life but can also cause volutrauma, barotrauma, atelectrauma, and inflammatory injury. For ARDS, guideline-based care uses lower tidal volumes—typically 4–8 mL/kg predicted body weight, not actual weight—and limits inspiratory pressures. Plateau pressure is assessed to help keep lung stress within the prescribed protective target.

Positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) helps prevent alveolar collapse and can improve oxygenation, but excessive PEEP can overdistend lung, reduce venous return, lower blood pressure, and raise right-ventricular workload. FiO₂ and PEEP are titrated together to adequate—not excessive—oxygenation. Permissive hypercapnia may be accepted in selected clients to preserve lung protection, but only within an authorized plan and with attention to pH and contraindications.

Tidal volume follows height and sex-based predicted body weight
Using actual body weight can deliver excessive tidal volume to a client with obesity. Verify the documented height, predicted-body-weight calculation, delivered tidal volume, plateau pressure, PEEP, FiO₂, and response.

Prone positioning is a team procedure

Prolonged prone positioning improves outcomes in appropriately selected severe ARDS by recruiting dorsal lung regions and improving V/Q matching. It requires a trained team, checklist, airway leader, and a plan for emergency return to supine. The RN secures the endotracheal tube and all lines and drains, protects eyes and pressure points, manages enteral feeding according to protocol, and reassesses hemodynamics and oxygenation.

Inspect the face, chest, pelvis, knees, and device sites; reposition the head and arms according to the schedule; provide eye care; and watch for tube displacement, brachial plexus injury, pressure injury, edema, obstruction, dysrhythmia, or instability. Improved saturation does not remove these safety responsibilities.

Read ventilator alarms as clinical clues

High-pressure alarms indicate increased resistance or reduced compliance. Causes include coughing, biting, secretions, kinked tubing, bronchospasm, water in the circuit, pneumothorax, worsening pulmonary edema or ARDS, abdominal pressure, or fighting the ventilator. Low-pressure or low-volume alarms often indicate disconnection, circuit leak, cuff leak, tube displacement, or inadequate delivered breath.

Go to the bedside and assess the client first. Check chest movement, breath sounds, oxygenation, hemodynamics, tube depth and security, circuit connections, kinks, secretions, and ventilator display. Do not silence an alarm without finding its cause. If the client is unstable and the ventilator or circuit is suspected, disconnect from the ventilator and provide manual ventilation with an oxygen source using the approved emergency process while calling for help.

Protect the artificial airway

Verify endotracheal or tracheostomy tube depth, security, cuff pressure monitoring, and placement confirmation according to protocol. Assess bilateral breath sounds, chest movement, exhaled carbon dioxide when used, oral and skin integrity, and signs of displacement. Restrain only under legal and organizational requirements after individualized alternatives; prevent unplanned extubation through comfort, communication, sedation assessment, and device security.

Suction when assessment indicates retained secretions—not by an automatic schedule. Preoxygenate when required, use aseptic or closed-system technique as applicable, limit each pass, avoid routine saline instillation, and monitor oxygenation, rhythm, blood pressure, and tolerance. A sudden inability to pass the suction catheter suggests tube obstruction or kinking and requires urgent escalation.

Prevent ventilator-associated harm

Use hand hygiene, oral care, head-of-bed elevation when not contraindicated, aspiration-risk reduction, appropriate subglottic secretion drainage when available, and daily evaluation for reducing sedation and ventilatory support. Avoid routine circuit changes without indication and drain condensate away from the client while preventing staff exposure.

Mechanical ventilation also increases delirium, immobility, sleep disruption, weakness, venous thromboembolism, stress-ulcer, corneal, skin, and communication risks. Coordinate analgesia-first comfort, the lightest safe sedation, delirium prevention, sleep support, early mobility, nutrition, communication aids, and prophylaxis based on individualized risk and protocol.

Evaluate readiness to liberate every day

Ventilator liberation begins with treating the cause and minimizing avoidable support. Daily coordinated spontaneous awakening and spontaneous breathing assessments can identify readiness. A spontaneous breathing trial evaluates whether the client can sustain breathing with reduced support; it is not the same as extubation readiness.

Before extubation, assess oxygenation and ventilation, hemodynamic stability, mental status, cough strength, secretion burden, airway protection, upper-airway risk, and the reintubation plan. During and after a trial or extubation, watch for tachypnea, distress, diaphoresis, dysrhythmia, blood-pressure change, hypoxemia, rising carbon dioxide, fatigue, stridor, or inability to clear secretions. Failure is clinical information, not blame.

Apply clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Assess airway, speech, mentation, effort, breath sounds, secretions, oxygen device, saturation, hemodynamics, blood gases, imaging, ventilator values and alarms, sedation, and baseline reserve.
  2. Analyze cues: Separate oxygenation failure from ventilation failure, identify the cause, distinguish client deterioration from equipment failure, and connect ARDS physiology with compliance and shunt.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Airway obstruction or displacement, apnea, severe hypoxemia, tension pneumothorax, failed noninvasive support, shock, and ventilator disconnection require immediate action.
  4. Generate solutions: Open and support the airway, titrate oxygen, remove obstruction, treat the cause, select safe ventilatory support, apply lung protection, and prepare rescue resources.
  5. Take action: Go to the bedside for alarms, support manual ventilation if necessary, escalate before arrest, use protocol-directed positioning and suction, and protect every line and pressure point.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Trend effort, mentation, oxygenation, carbon dioxide and pH, hemodynamics, ventilator synchrony and pressures, skin and airway integrity, infection risk, mobility, and readiness to reduce support.

Clinical example

A client with sepsis and bilateral opacities is intubated for worsening hypoxemia. The high-pressure alarm activates and saturation falls. The RN immediately assesses the client, notes diminished unilateral breath sounds and hypotension, calls for emergency help, and evaluates tube position and the circuit while preparing manual ventilation. The pattern raises concern for tension pneumothorax rather than “just secretions,” so definitive bedside treatment is not delayed. After stabilization, the RN rechecks predicted-body-weight tidal volume, plateau pressure, PEEP, FiO₂, synchrony, hemodynamics, and the cause of ARDS.

Original educational synthesis. Respiratory-failure diagnosis, oxygen targets, noninvasive support, intubation, ventilator settings, suction, prone positioning, sedation, weaning, extubation, and emergency airway management require current client data, authorized orders, exact equipment instructions, local protocols, respiratory and critical-care expertise, and qualified supervision. This lesson is not medical advice, clinical decision support, certification, continuing education, or an official ATS, AARC, NHLBI, CDC, or NCSBN product.
